title: Women in the reform
hookLine: women taught, marched, wrote and went to jail in these movements

cards: Look closely at a group photograph from the reform years: rows of men in dark turbans, staring straight at the camera. Look at the edges. Behind them, half in shadow, a woman in a white chunni.

In some pictures she isn't there at all, and yet she cooked the langar the jatha ate before it left, sewed the banners, ran the school, wrote letters to the newspaper, and sometimes walked in the jatha herself.
These last weeks have been full of men's names.

teach.b: Earlier in this block came the school for girls at Ferozepur.
Bibi Harnam Kaur worked alongside her husband, Bhai Takht Singh, to build it, and women like her taught there, so girls could read Gurmukhi and the Guru Granth Sahib for themselves.
Women wrote too: poems, essays and letters in the Sikh papers of the time, arguing for girls' education and for reform.
In the Ghadar story, Bibi Gulab Kaur is remembered as a woman who went back to India to work for its freedom when her husband turned back, and who was imprisoned for it.

teach.h: WOMEN WHO MARCHED AND WERE JAILED.
teach.b: In the gurdwara campaigns, women joined the morchas and the jathas, and histories of the Akali movement name women, such as Bibi Kishan Kaur Kaunke, among those arrested. The line from Sundri's day belongs here too.
At Ang 473 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak asks why a woman should be called lesser, when from her kings are born.

That line was in the scripture long before any reform movement, and some historians read the women of these years as holding the panth to its own scripture. The records are thinner for them than for the men.
Names have been lost, and sources sometimes mention a woman only as someone's wife or mother. That's part of the story too, and why remembering the names that survive matters.

how: Sikh histories, gurdwara programs and community events tell the stories of women in the reform movements, and the girls' schools and women's organizations of those years are remembered as part of that work.

games.q: you're Gulab Kaur. you and your husband planned to return to India to work for its freedom, and now he's turned back. what do you do?
o: wait for the movement to send for you.
games.why: she is remembered as going back without him, working for the movement, and being imprisoned for it.

practice: Bring to mind one woman who changed something for others and rarely got the credit: a grandmother who kept a family going, a teacher, an organizer, someone whose work everyone relied on and nobody thanked.
Say her name silently, picture what she did, and let her be seen, if only by you. If you pray, hold her in mind with Waheguru on the breath out.

wordCard.voice: Bibi, a respectful title for a Sikh woman: the women who taught, wrote, marched and went to jail in the reform movements, whose names the records too often lose. Today's word.
